title: What is Apache Pulsar and how does it differ architecturally from Kafka — a decoupled design (stateless brokers + Apache BookKeeper for storage + a metadata store) vs Kafka's broker-owns-its-storage model, first-class multi-tenancy via tenant/namespace/topic, built-in geo-replication, and support for BOTH streaming (pub/sub) and queue (competing-consumer) semantics with built-in retry + dead-letter topics — and when would you still prefer Kafka (more mature ecosystem, existing infra, raw throughput)?
shortTitle: Apache Pulsar versus Kafka — architecture and when to prefer each
topicTitle: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS vs Pulsar

s1_definition.profdef: Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform with a layered, decoupled architecture that separates serving from storage. Stateless Pulsar brokers handle client connections and message routing but store nothing locally; durable storage is delegated to Apache BookKeeper nodes called bookies, and cluster metadata lives in a separate metadata store such as ZooKeeper or etcd. This contrasts with Kafka, where each broker owns the partition data on its own local disks. Pulsar adds first-class multi-tenancy through a tenant/namespace/topic hierarchy, built-in geo-replication, and native support for both streaming (pub-sub) and queuing (competing-consumer) semantics with built-in retry and dead-letter topics.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine two ways to run the vaults of National Bank of India. In the Kafka model, each branch manager keeps the gold in a safe inside their own office — if that office is overwhelmed with customers, moving the gold to another office is slow. In the Pulsar model, the branch managers (brokers) only serve customers at the counter, while the actual gold sits in a shared central vault building (BookKeeper) nearby. If one manager gets busy, another manager instantly serves the same customers because none of them personally hold the gold. Pulsar also keeps separate floors for each client company (multi-tenancy) and automatically copies the vault to another city (geo-replication).
s1_definition.oneliner: Pulsar decouples stateless brokers from BookKeeper storage for fast scaling and multi-tenancy, while Kafka's broker-owns-storage model wins on maturity, ecosystem, and raw throughput.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform with a layered, decoupled architecture that separates serving from storage. Stateless Pulsar brokers handle client connections and message routing but store nothing locally; durable storage is delegated to Apache BookKeeper nodes called bookies, and cluster metadata lives in a separate metadata store such as ZooKeeper or etcd. This contrasts with Kafka, where each broker owns the partition data on its own local disks. Pulsar adds first-class multi-tenancy through a tenant/namespace/topic hierarchy, built-in geo-replication, and native support for both streaming (pub-sub) and queuing (competing-consumer) semantics with built-in retry and dead-letter topics.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine two ways to run the vaults of National Bank of India. In the Kafka model, each branch manager keeps the gold in a safe inside their own office — if that office is overwhelmed with customers, moving the gold to another office is slow. In the Pulsar model, the branch managers (brokers) only serve customers at the counter, while the actual gold sits in a shared central vault building (BookKeeper) nearby. If one manager gets busy, another manager instantly serves the same customers because none of them personally hold the gold. Pulsar also keeps separate floors for each client company (multi-tenancy) and automatically copies the vault to another city (geo-replication).

**One line to remember:** Pulsar decouples stateless brokers from BookKeeper storage for fast scaling and multi-tenancy, while Kafka's broker-owns-storage model wins on maturity, ecosystem, and raw throughput.

sections.s2_technical:
The defining architectural difference is the separation of compute and storage. In Kafka, a broker both serves clients and stores partition log segments on its own disk. When you add a broker to scale, Kafka must physically rebalance partition data across the network, which is slow and I/O heavy. In Pulsar, brokers are stateless routers; they own no data. Storage is handled by BookKeeper bookies that store message segments (ledgers) spread across many bookies. Because a broker holds no data, you can add or remove brokers in seconds, and if a broker dies another broker immediately picks up its topics without copying any data.

BookKeeper stores data as segments rather than as one long per-partition file. A Pulsar topic's data is split into many ledgers distributed across bookies, so no single node owns an entire topic's history. This makes storage scaling independent of serving — you add bookies for more storage and brokers for more throughput, separately. Kafka's tiered storage feature narrows this gap by offloading old segments to object storage, but the core broker still owns the active data.

Multi-tenancy is first-class in Pulsar through the tenant/namespace/topic hierarchy. A topic name looks like `persistent://banking-tenant/payments/transfers`. The tenant is an organization, the namespace is a grouping with its own policies (retention, quotas, access control), and the topic is the stream. This lets one Pulsar cluster safely host many isolated business units. Kafka has no native tenant concept; isolation is usually done with separate clusters or naming conventions plus ACLs.

Geo-replication is built into Pulsar at the namespace level. You enable replication to another cluster with a configuration change, and Pulsar handles the cross-region copy. Kafka achieves this with a separate tool, MirrorMaker 2, which is powerful but operationally heavier.

Messaging models differ too. Kafka is fundamentally a log with consumer groups, giving streaming pub-sub semantics; queue-style competing consumers are approximated with partitions. Pulsar natively supports multiple subscription types in the same topic: Exclusive and Failover subscriptions behave like streaming, while Shared and Key_Shared subscriptions behave like a traditional queue where multiple consumers compete for messages. Pulsar also ships built-in retry topics and dead-letter topics as a native feature, whereas in Kafka you typically add Spring Kafka's RetryableTopic or write your own.

The senior nuance is when to still choose Kafka. Kafka has a far more mature ecosystem — Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams, ksqlDB, Schema Registry, and enormous community and vendor support. If your organization already runs Kafka, has the operational expertise, and needs the highest raw sequential throughput on existing infrastructure, Kafka is the pragmatic choice. Pulsar shines when you need rapid elastic scaling, strong multi-tenancy, built-in geo-replication, and both queue and stream semantics in one platform, at the cost of operating the extra BookKeeper layer.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is evaluating whether to adopt Pulsar alongside or instead of Kafka, and the platform team must build a decision helper and a small abstraction that documents the architectural differences.

Problem 1 — During festival season the payments load spikes tenfold overnight, and the team needs to add serving capacity in seconds without a slow data rebalance. This is exactly where Pulsar's stateless brokers help — adding a broker needs no data movement because storage lives in BookKeeper.

Problem 2 — The bank runs a shared platform for its retail division, its wealth-management subsidiary, and a fintech partner, and each must be strictly isolated with its own quotas and retention. This is exactly Pulsar's first-class multi-tenancy through tenant/namespace/topic.

Problem 3 — Some workloads are streams (fraud analytics reading all events) and others are queues (one worker per statement job), and the team wants one platform for both with built-in dead-letter handling. This is exactly Pulsar's Shared and Key_Shared subscriptions plus native retry and dead-letter topics.

Problem 4 — The bank already runs a large, stable Kafka cluster with Kafka Connect and Schema Registry, and the highest-throughput trade feed must stay there. This is exactly when to still prefer Kafka — maturity, ecosystem, existing infrastructure, and raw throughput.

The mini-project is a platform-selection advisor. We build a `PlatformChoice` domain object, a `StreamingPlatformAdvisor` service that recommends Pulsar or Kafka based on scaling, tenancy, mixed semantics, and existing-infra flags, and two illustrative sender classes `PulsarSender` (showing the tenant/namespace/topic name) and `KafkaSender` (showing the flat topic name). The demo runs all four banking scenarios and logs the recommendation with the architectural reason.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four evaluation scenarios, each a set of boolean requirements.

Step 1 — The festival-spike scenario sets rapidElasticScaling true. The advisor returns Pulsar with the reason that stateless brokers plus BookKeeper storage let you add brokers in seconds with no data rebalance. The decision object lives in memory.

Step 2 — The multi-tenancy scenario sets multiTenancy true. The advisor returns Pulsar and explains the tenant/namespace/topic hierarchy. The `PulsarSender` then produces to persistent://banking-tenant/payments/transfers, showing the fully qualified topic name that encodes the tenant and namespace.

Step 3 — The mixed-semantics scenario sets mixedStreamAndQueue true. The advisor returns Pulsar and cites Shared and Key_Shared subscriptions that provide both streaming and queue behavior plus native dead-letter topics.

Step 4 — The existing-infra scenario sets existingKafkaInfra true, which the advisor checks first. It returns Kafka, citing the mature ecosystem, existing infrastructure, and raw throughput. The `KafkaSender` produces to the flat topic trade.feed with key SAV2001, illustrating that the broker owns the partition storage.

Step 5 — All four recommendations are logged with the architectural reason, giving a clear, auditable decision record the team can take to an architecture review.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform whose defining feature is a decoupled architecture that separates serving from storage. Pulsar brokers are stateless and own no data; they only route messages. Durable storage is handled by a separate layer, Apache BookKeeper, and cluster metadata lives in a metadata store like ZooKeeper or etcd. Kafka takes the opposite approach — each broker owns its partition data on local disk. That single difference drives most of the comparison.

Because Pulsar brokers hold no data, you can add or remove them in seconds with no slow data rebalance, which is ideal for sudden load spikes. Pulsar also offers first-class multi-tenancy through a tenant, namespace, and topic hierarchy, so one cluster can safely host isolated business units with their own quotas and retention. It has built-in geo-replication configured per namespace, and it natively supports both streaming pub-sub and queue-style competing-consumer semantics in the same topic through subscription types like Shared and Key_Shared, along with built-in retry and dead-letter topics.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, I would reach for Pulsar when I need rapid elastic scaling during festival spikes, strict multi-tenancy across the retail, wealth, and fintech-partner divisions, and a single platform that serves both stream and queue workloads with native dead-letter handling.

That said, I would still prefer Kafka in several situations, and I say this honestly in interviews. Kafka has a far more mature ecosystem with Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams, ksqlDB, and Schema Registry, enormous community and vendor support, and the highest raw sequential throughput. If the organization already runs Kafka and has the operational expertise, the pragmatic choice is usually to stay with Kafka, especially for the highest-throughput trade feeds. Pulsar's power comes at the cost of operating the extra BookKeeper layer, so I treat it as a deliberate trade-off rather than a default.

keyPoints: Kafka vs RabbitMQ: log-based vs message broker, persistence vs routing
Kafka vs SQS: self-managed vs managed, ordering vs simplicity
Kafka vs Pulsar: similar architecture, Pulsar has tiered storage
Choose based on: throughput, ordering, retention, operational complexity
